label: Almost Complex Structures
notes: Welcome to Lecture 12, spanning printed pages 65 through 71. Today we add a third actor to symplectic geometry: an endomorphism J of the tangent bundle that squares to minus the identity. Stress that J, the form omega, and a metric g form a compatible triple we will assemble piece by piece.

label: Three Linear Geometries
notes: Open by contrasting three structures on a single vector space: a skew nondegenerate form, a symmetric positive metric, and a square root of minus one. Each is familiar alone. The lecture's thesis is that compatibility braids them so any two determine the third, and that is the picture students should carry forward.

label: Definition of J
notes: Define an almost complex structure as a smooth bundle map J on the tangent spaces with J squared equal to minus the identity. Emphasize that this is pointwise linear algebra varying smoothly, and that it makes each tangent space a complex vector space where multiplication by i is the action of J.

label: J Rotates by 90 Degrees
notes: Use the picture to make J concrete: it sends a tangent vector to a perpendicular one, and applying it twice reverses the vector. Walk the class around the loop v, Jv, minus v, minus Jv. This ninety-degree quarter turn is the geometric heart of the identity J squared equals minus the identity.

label: Taming and Compatibility
notes: Introduce the two conditions relating J to omega. Taming asks only that omega of v with Jv be strictly positive on nonzero vectors. Compatibility adds that J preserves omega, meaning omega of Jv and Jw equals omega of v and w. Compatible structures are exactly the tame ones that are also symplectic.

label: The Compatible Metric
notes: Here is the payoff: a compatible J turns omega into a Riemannian metric by g of v and w equals omega of v with Jw. Symmetry comes from compatibility, and positive definiteness is precisely the taming inequality. Show students the closed triangle where omega, g, and J each recover from the other two.

label: Positivity Becomes a Metric
notes: Dwell on why positivity matters. The diagonal value g of v with itself equals omega of v with Jv, which the taming condition forces to be positive. Geometrically the unit balls of g are honest ellipses. Connect this to the notebook, where the minimum eigenvalue of the compatible metric is the computational witness of positivity.

label: Existence via Polar Decomposition
notes: State the existence theorem: every symplectic manifold admits compatible almost complex structures. Sketch the proof. Choose any metric, represent omega by a skew-adjoint operator A, take the positive square root of A times its adjoint, and normalize. Polar decomposition canonically extracts J from that factorization.

label: The Space of Compatible J
notes: Explain that compatible structures are not unique but form a contractible space. The construction depends continuously on the chosen metric, and the metrics form a convex set, so the compatible J's deform into one another without obstruction. Contractibility is what lets us treat a compatible J as essentially canonical in later proofs.

label: A Path of Compatible Structures
notes: Walk through the notebook experiment. Conjugating the standard J by symplectic scalings produces a family J of s. The metric ellipses visibly change shape, yet the compatibility residual stays at machine zero and the positivity floor stays above zero. This finite-dimensional path illustrates the contractibility statement concretely.

label: Recap and the U(n) Picture
notes: Close by gathering threads. Compatibility intersects the orthogonal, symplectic, and complex-linear groups, and their common intersection is the unitary group. Remind students that omega, g, and J form one compatible triple, that such triples always exist, and that the choice is contractible. This sets up Kahler geometry in the lectures ahead.
